title: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:

Consider a infinite-horizon1 Markov decision process \(\mathcal M\) with states \(s \in \mathcal S\), actions \(a \in \mathcal A\), rewards \(r \in \mathbb R\), discount factor \(\gamma \in (0, 1)\), transition dynamics \(p(s', r \mid s, a)\), and initial state distribution \(\rho_0(s)\). In reinforcement learning, we learn a policy \(\pi \in \Pi\) that maximizes the expected cumulative discounted rewards \[
J(\pi) \mathrel{\mathop{=}\limits^{\text{def}}}\operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{s_0 \sim \rho_0} }\!\left[ V^{\pi}(s_0) \right].
\tag{1}\] While there are many methods to solve this, a popular approach is using policy gradient methods (see Sutton & Barto, chapter 13) which use gradient descent to directly optimize \(J(\pi)\) using \(\nabla_\boldsymbol\theta J(\pi)\), where the policy \(\pi(a \mid s)\) is parametized by some vector \(\boldsymbol\theta\in \mathbb R^d\) (e.g. a neural network).

title: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
2.1 Deriving the Surrogate Advantage
Consider an update moving from policy \(\pi_\text{old}\) to policy \(\pi\). If we want to ensure the optimizer takes a good step, we need to evaluate \(J(\pi)\) and check that it’s greater than \(J(\pi_\text{old})\). However, this is exceedingly expensive, which motivates the question of can we evaluate the performance of \(\pi\) using only \(\pi_\text{old}\)? To do this, we’ll define a new objective function called the surrogate advantage.
Starting with the expected cumulative discounted rewards \(J(\pi)\), we can replace \(r_t\) with \(A^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_t, a_t)\): \[
\begin{alignat*}{2}
J(\pi) &= \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{s_0 \sim \rho_0} }\!\left[  V^{\pi}(s_0)  \right] \\
&= \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{\pi} }\!\left[  \sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^t r_t  \right] && \text{(definition of $V^{\pi}$)} \\
&= \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{\pi} }\!\left[  \sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^t\big( r_t + \textcolor{WildStrawberry}{ V^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_{t+1}) - V^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_{t+1}) } \big)  \right] \\
&= \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{\pi} }\!\left[  \sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^t\big( \textcolor{WildStrawberry}{ Q^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_t, a_t) } - V^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_{t+1}) \big)  \right] && \text{(definition of $Q^{\pi_\text{old}}$)} \\
&= \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{\pi} }\!\left[  \sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^t \big(\textcolor{WildStrawberry}{ A^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_t, a_t) + V^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_t) } - V^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_{t+1})\big)  \right] \qquad && \text{(definition of $A^{\pi_\text{old}}$)} \\
&= \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{\pi} }\!\left[  \sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^t A^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_t, a_t)  \right] + \textcolor{WildStrawberry}{ \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{s_0 \sim \rho_0} }\!\left[  V^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_0)  \right] } && \text{(telescoping sum)} \\
&= \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{\pi} }\!\left[  \sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^t A^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_t, a_t)  \right] + J(\pi_\text{old}).
\end{alignat*}
\] This result is known as the performance difference lemma: \[
\mathcal L(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) \mathrel{\mathop{=}\limits^{\text{def}}}J(\pi) - J(\pi_\text{old}) = \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{\pi} }\!\left[  \sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^tA^{\pi_\text{old}}(s_t, a_t)  \right].
\] Since \(J(\pi_\text{old})\) is independent of \(\pi\), we can optimize \(\mathcal L(\pi, \pi_\text{old})\) instead of \(J(\pi)\) to find the optimal policy. Importantly, we see that we only need to evaluate the advantage of \(\pi_\text{old}\) instead of \(\pi\)!
However, to calculate the expectation we still need Monte Carlo rollouts from \(\pi\) which is inefficient. To manipulate the expectation, it’s easier to consider individual states as opposed to entire trajectories. To this end we introduce the state distribution \[
\rho_\pi(s) \mathrel{\mathop{=}\limits^{\text{def}}}(1 - \gamma) \sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^t \Pr(s_t = s \mid s_0 \sim \rho_0, \pi)
\] and rewrite the performance difference2 as \[
\mathcal L(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) = \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{s \sim \rho_\pi \\ a \sim \pi(\cdot \mid s)} }\!\left[  A^{\pi_\text{old}}(s, a)  \right].
\] In this formulation, there are two distributions being sampled from in the expectation: \(\rho_\pi\) and \(\pi(\cdot \mid s)\).
2 If it’s not clear why this is possible, there are only two operations happening here: we introduce and distribute the fraction \(\frac{1 - \gamma}{1 - \gamma}\), and we move the policy from the expectation to the probability term in \(\rho_\pi\). The logic is similar to that of the policy gradient theorem proof presented in Sutton & Barto chapter 13.3 We assume that \(\pi\) and \(\pi_\text{old}\) are both well-behaved, i.e. \(\pi(a \mid s) \neq 0\) for all \(a \in \mathcal A\) and \(s \in \mathcal S\).Of these, \(\pi(\cdot \mid s)\) has a closed-form, e.g. a neural network. Forward passes in neural networks are efficient to compute, so we can use importance sampling to sample from \(\pi_\text{old}(\cdot \mid s)\) instead3: \[
\mathcal L(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) = \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{s \sim \rho_\pi \\ \textcolor{WildStrawberry}{ a \sim \pi_\text{old}(\cdot \mid s) }} }\!\left[  \textcolor{WildStrawberry}{ \frac{\pi(a \mid s)}{\pi_\text{old}(a \mid s)} } A^{\pi_\text{old}}(s,a)  \right].
\]
Unfortunately, \(\rho_\pi\) has no closed-form solution meaning we can’t use importance sampling to sample from \(\rho_{\pi_\text{old}}\).
If we consider how policy gradient methods work, they generally take iterative steps leading to a sequence of policies \(\{\pi_1, \pi_2, \dots, \pi_k\}\). Intuitively, each consecutive policy should be decently similar, i.e. \(\pi \approx \pi_\text{old}\). If we make that assumption, then it follows that \(\rho_\pi \approx \rho_{\pi_\text{old}}\). If we replace \(\rho_\pi\) with \(\rho_{\pi_\text{old}}\) in the performance difference function, then we get the surrogate advantage objective \[
\widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) = \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{\textcolor{WildStrawberry}{ s \sim \rho_{\pi_\text{old}} } \\ a \sim \pi_\text{old}(\cdot \mid s)} }\!\left[  \frac{\pi(a \mid s)}{\pi_\text{old}(a \mid s)} A^{\pi_\text{old}}(s,a)  \right].
\tag{2}\] In the surrogate advantage, our expectation is over exclusively \(\pi_\text{old}\), meaning we can reuse Monte Carlo rollouts of \(\pi_\text{old}\) without simulating \(\pi\). Additionally, so long as \(\pi \approx \pi_\text{old}\) we know that \(J(\pi) \approx \widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) + J(\pi_\text{old})\), meaning that we can estimate \(J(\pi)\) while only using \(\pi_\text{old}\). This is exactly what we wanted from our new objective!

title: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
2.2 The Monotone Convergence Guarantee
From Section 2.1, we know that \(w\mathcal L(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) \approx \mathcal L(\pi, \pi_\text{old})\) only if \(\pi \approx \pi_\text{old}\), so we need some way to formalize when this is true. The standard way to measure the similarity of probability distributions is the Kullback-Leibler divergence \[
D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old}(\cdot \mid s) \,\|\, \pi(\cdot \mid s) \vphantom{\big(} \right) \mathrel{\mathop{=}\limits^{\text{def}}}\operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{a \sim \pi_\text{old}(\cdot \mid s)} }\!\left[ \log\left(\frac{\pi_\text{old}(a \mid s)}{\pi(a \mid s)}\right) \right].
\]
However, the policy can change for each state, so we need a way to aggregate the KL divergence into a single measurement. Mathematically, it’s easiest to use the worst-case divergence \[
D_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right) = \max_{s \in \mathcal S} D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old}(\cdot \mid s) \,\|\, \pi(\cdot \mid s) \vphantom{\big(} \right).
\] Intuitively, this states that even if \(\pi\) and \(\pi_\text{old}\) normally take the same action, if there’s even one state where they differ that will be reflected in \(D_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\). This makes sense for reinforcement learning, where there’s often a few critical states (e.g. a cliff that the agent could fall off of), and we may not be sure which states those are.
Using the worst-case KL divergence, the paper Trust Region Policy Optimization by Schulman et. al. proves the monotone convergence theorem:






Monotone Convergence Theorem




Theorem 1 (Monotone Convergence) For two policies \(\pi, \pi_\text{old}\in \Pi\) we have that \[
\mathcal L(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) \geq \widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) - CD_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right),
\] where \(C\) is a function of the discount factor \(\gamma\) and the maximum advantage of \(\pi_\text{old}\).



This means that if we use the update step \[
\pi_\text{new}\gets \mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{\pi \in \Pi}\; \widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) - CD_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)
\tag{3}\] we will always converge to the optimal policy since Equation 3 is bounded by zero when \(\pi=\pi_\text{old}\), i.e. it must be true that \(J(\pi_0) \leq J(\pi_1) \leq \cdots \leq J(\pi_k)\).
This theorem clearly fixes the issue of knowing when \(\pi \approx \pi_\text{old}\), since the \(CD_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\) acts as a penalty parameter, reducing our improvement as we get further from \(\pi_\text{old}\). However, this also fixes the original policy gradient problem of high variance! Since we now control how far away \(\pi\) and \(\pi_\text{old}\) are, we can be confident that our step is a good one!
This is why the penalty term is the worst-case KL divergence, since it measures the distance in policy space and not the parameter space. If we were to instead use a parameter space measure like the \(\ell_2\) norm \(\frac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old}\|^2\), the resulting policies could still be different since they’re non-linear in \(\boldsymbol\theta\). In essence, \(\boldsymbol\theta\approx \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old}\) does not imply that \(\pi \approx \pi_\text{old}\), which was causing the high variance of the policy gradient updates!
However, while this update is theoretically sound it’s difficult to implement. The first issue is that since the \(C\) parameter depends on the maximum advantage of \(\pi_\text{old}\), it’s intractable to calculate for large or unbounded state spaces. Ideally, we could set \(C\) as a global hyperparameter, but this proves to be difficult. Intuitively, this is because \(C\) directly affects both the divergence term and the surrogate advantage term. For one update, a value of \(C = 10^{-3}\) could be large relative to the surrogate advantage, and for another it could be small, even if the worst-case divergence is the same.
In practice, we rewrite Equation 3 as an equivalent dual constrained optimization problem \[
\pi_\text{new}\gets \mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{\pi \in \Pi}\; \widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) \text{ such that }D_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right) \leq \delta,
\tag{4}\] which replaces the \(C\) parameter with a \(\delta\) parameter that also depends on \(\gamma\) and the maximum advantage. However, because the \(\delta\) parameter is exclusively in the constraint it’s easier to set as a global hyperparameter. Intuitively, since it doesn’t impact the surrogate advantage it will always directly bound the worst-case divergence the same, no matter where in policy space you are.

title: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
2.3 Quadratic Trust Region Optimization
Unfortunately, it’s not clear how to actually solve for the update in Equation 4. Theoretically, there are closed form solutions for constrained optimization problems with linear objectives and quadratic constraints, so if we approximate \(\widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old})\) with a linear function and \(D_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\) with a quadratic function we can use the closed-form update. Additionally, at each update we’ve calculated and simulated \(\pi_\text{old}\), so we have access to Monte Carlo rollouts and an advantage estimate. Since we’re only considering policies \(\pi\) that are close to \(\pi_\text{old}\) due to the worst-case divergence constraint, we can use Taylor series approximations to estimate \(\widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old})\) and \(D_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\).

2.3.1 Approximating \(D_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\)
Since \(D_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\) is a maximum over the state space, we need to enumerate every element which is intractable for large or unbounded state spaces. In policy gradient methods, we generally interact with the environment using Monte Carlo rollouts, so let’s instead consider the expected divergence \[
\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right) \mathrel{\mathop{=}\limits^{\text{def}}}\operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{s \sim \rho_{\pi_\text{old}}} }\!\left[ D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old}(\cdot \mid s) \,\|\, \pi(\cdot \mid s) \vphantom{\big(} \right) \right].
\] If we approximate \(D_\text{KL}^{\max} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\) with \(\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\) then it’s possible that this misses some key states with high divergence, but overall it will accomplish the same result of stopping the new policy from straying too far from the old policy.
The second-order Taylor approximation of \(\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\) centered at \(\pi=\pi_\text{old}\) is \[
\begin{align*}
\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right) &\approx \left[\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\right]_{\pi=\pi_\text{old}} \\
&\quad +\; (\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old})^\top \nabla_\boldsymbol\theta\left[\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\right]_{\pi = \pi_\text{old}} \\
&\quad +\; \frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old})^\top\nabla_\boldsymbol\theta^2\left[\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\right]_{\pi = \pi_\text{old}}(\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old})
\end{align*}
\] It’s clear that \(\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi_\text{old} \vphantom{\big(} \right) = 0\), which drops out. Additionally, some algebra shows that \(\nabla_\boldsymbol\theta\left[\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\right]_{\pi=\pi_\text{old}} = \mathbf 0\), causing the first-order term to drop out as well. Thus, the second-order approximation is completely determined by the Hessian matrix \[
\mathbf H= \nabla_\boldsymbol\theta^2\left[\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\right]_{\pi=\pi_\text{old}} = -\operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{s \sim \rho_{\pi_\text{old}} \\ a \sim \pi_\text{old}(\cdot \mid s)} }\!\left[ \nabla_\boldsymbol\theta^2 \log \pi(a \mid s) \right].
\] Thus, our final approximation is \[
\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right) \approx \frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old})^\top \mathbf H(\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old}).
\tag{5}\]


2.3.2 Approximating \(\widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old})\)
The first-order Taylor expansion centered at \(\pi=\pi_\text{old}\) (ignoring the constant term since it doesn’t afffect optimization) is \[
\begin{align*}
\mathbf g&= \nabla_\boldsymbol\theta\widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) \\
&= \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{s \sim \rho_{\pi_\text{old}} \\ a \sim \pi_\text{old}(\cdot \mid s)} }\!\left[ \nabla_\boldsymbol\theta\frac{\pi(a \mid s)}{\pi_\text{old}(a \mid s)} A^{\pi_\text{old}}(s, a) \right] \\
&= \operatorname*{\mathbb{E}}_{ \substack{s \sim \rho_{\pi_\text{old}} \\ a \sim \pi_\text{old}(\cdot \mid s)} }\!\left[ A^{\pi_\text{old}}(s, a) \nabla_\boldsymbol\theta\log \pi(a \mid s) \right].
\end{align*}
\] This is actually the same as \(\nabla_\boldsymbol\theta J(\pi_\text{old})\) from the policy gradient theorem (see Sutton & Barto, chapter 13), providing further justification that \(\widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old})\) is a good stand-in for \(J(\pi)\). Our final estimate is then \[
\widetilde{\mathcal L}(\pi, \pi_\text{old}) \approx (\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old})^\top\mathbf g.
\tag{6}\]


2.3.3 Solving the Update Step






How do we efficiently calculate the inverse of the Hessian?



Calculating \(\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf g\) is normally \(\mathcal O(d^3)\) time. Instead, since the Hessian is the expected Fisher information matrix of the policy we can implement Hessian products as the operator \[
\mathbf H\mathbf x= \nabla_\boldsymbol\theta\!\left[ \left(\nabla_\boldsymbol\theta\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\right)^\top\mathbf x\right].
\] Using a Krylov subspace method like conjugate gradient, we can use this to calculate \(\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf g\) with a time complexity of roughly \(\mathcal O\!\left(d\sqrt{\kappa(\mathbf H)}\right)\). Importantly, this only requires access to \(\nabla_\boldsymbol\theta\log \pi(a \mid s)\), which is easy to calculate for even complex policies using automatic differentiation.


Using the approximations Equation 6 and Equation 5, we form the update step \[
\boldsymbol\theta_\text{new}\gets \mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{\boldsymbol\theta\in \mathbb R^d}\, \mathbf g^\top(\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old}) \text{ such that }\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old})^\top\mathbf H(\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old}) \leq \delta
\] which has the closed-form solution \[
\boldsymbol\theta_\text{new}\gets \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old}+ \left(\sqrt{\frac{2 \delta}{\mathbf g^\top\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf g}}\right) \mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf g
\] Interestingly, this has the form of a natural gradient update, which is similar to a standard gradient descent update but accounts for the curvature of the policy space. However, since we approximated \(\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\), it’s possible that \(\boldsymbol\theta_\text{new}\) may not satisfy the constraint. Luckily this is simple to fix with a backtracking line search (see Nocedal & Wright chapter 3), where we introduce some \(\alpha \in (0, 1]\) and choose the largest \(\alpha\) such that \[
\boldsymbol\theta_\text{new}\gets \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old}+ \alpha\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2 \delta}{\mathbf g^\top\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf g}}\right) \mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf g
\tag{7}\] satisfies the expected divergence constraint. Now we have an update that we can efficiently calculate that approximately satisfies Theorem 1!

section: 2.4 Comparing KL Divergence to Euclidean Distance
text:
2.4 Comparing KL Divergence to Euclidean Distance
To visualize this, let’s consider an MDP with a single state \(\mathcal S= \{s\}\) and two actions \(\mathcal A= \{ a_1, a_2\}\). We’ll visualize a stochastic policy \(\pi\) with two parameters \(x, y \in \mathbb R\).
On the left of Figure 1 we plot the contours of \(\pi_{x,y}(a = a_1 \mid s)\), i.e. the probability that we take action \(a_1\) when \(\pi\) is parameterized by different \(x, y\) values. On the right we consider a specific policy \(\pi_\text{old}\) parameterized by \(x=1\) and \(y=1.1\) and plot the KL divergence of this policy against the KL divergence of other policies.
Using standard \(\ell_2\) regularized policy gradient methods, a REINFORCE update would correspond to finding the optimal policy in the constrainted \(\ell_2\) ball \(\color[RGB]{216,27,96}{ \frac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old}\|^2 \leq \delta }\). Notice how there’s high variance in the KL divergence values inside of this ball, implying that the update may not be stable. We can see on the left that the probability values \(\pi(a = a_1 \mid s)\) also change rapidly inside this region.
Compared against the ball of bounded KL divergence \(\color[RGB]{255,193,7}{ \overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right) \leq \delta }\), we see they are aligned very differently, and that there’s a long stretch of polcies that would be considered stable updates with similar policy values and thus bounded importance sampling ratios. Of course, we can’t calculate \(\overline D_\text{KL}^{} \!\left( \vphantom{\big(} \pi_\text{old} \,\|\, \pi \vphantom{\big(} \right)\) directly, so we consider the quadratic approximation \(\color[RGB]{213,94,0}{ \frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old})^\top\mathbf H(\boldsymbol\theta- \boldsymbol\theta_\text{old}) \leq \delta }\), which aligns much better with the true stable region.






Figure 1: A visualization of the KL divergence constraint compared to the standard Euclidean constraint.

title: Trust Region Policy Optimization
text:
2.5 What Have we Accomplished?
We now have Equation 7 which we can solve efficiently by only evaluating and sampling from \(\pi_\text{old}\). This update is guaranteed to satisfy the expected divergence constraint in Equation 4 due to the backtracking line search, but uses a first-order approximation (Equation 6) of the surrogate advantage. Assuming that this approximation is good enough, the monotone convergence theorem (Theorem 1) guarantees that this update will converge, fixing our issue with vanilla policy gradients!
